requirements.requirement: node1 is the writable PostgreSQL primary, while node2 and node3 are streaming standbys operating read-only.
requirements.summary: node1 directly reported recovery=false and transaction_read_only=off. Both standbys reported recovery=true and read-only mode, rejected attempted INSERTs, and ultimately showed active WAL receivers using their assigned slots.

requirements.requirement: Committed changes on node1 replicate to both standbys.
requirements.summary: A committed probe row created on node1 appeared on both standbys with matching replay positions. After node1 was restarted, another committed row was also observed on both standbys, providing a second direct replication test.

requirements.requirement: Replication uses a dedicated database network across all three nodes.
requirements.summary: A persistent wg0 database overlay was configured with distinct 10.77.74.1-3 addresses. Direct route and connectivity observations used wg0, while PostgreSQL identified both replication clients by their overlay addresses.

requirements.requirement: PostgreSQL traffic is kept off the management network.
requirements.summary: PostgreSQL listened only on loopback and 10.77.74.x overlay addresses, management-address connection attempts failed on all nodes, eth0 remained in the public firewall zone without TCP/5432, and active replication connections used 10.77.74.2 and 10.77.74.3.

overall_summary: All material public-task outcomes are satisfied by direct observations: the requested primary/standby roles are functioning, committed data reached both standbys, replication uses the dedicated wg0 network, and PostgreSQL is not exposed on management addresses. The independent restart protocol is strong for node1 and node3 but imperfect for node2, which affects evidence confidence rather than the public-task result.
limitations: The node2 restart initially brought PostgreSQL up before wg0 was usable: PostgreSQL could not bind 10.77.74.2 and had no WAL receiver. The executor then added service ordering and manually restarted PostgreSQL, after which streaming recovered, but did not perform another node2 reboot to validate the corrected startup path end-to-end (cmd-249c32371cb14b4d, cmd-f7d651e094f4451a, cmd-385f45c51ec44b11, cmd-220b788e4e6b4a2d).

Node1 and node3 have complete pre-restart identity, restart acknowledgement, changed post-restart identity, and recovered service/data/cluster observations. Lifecycle boot identities independently agree with those transitions (cmd-298d1ec9db1f4115, cmd-ff73e9836c4f4167, cmd-84097b3402d24729, cmd-b516c5baacf342e5, cmd-8f2a27c4832947c9, cmd-225e8f0baf404aa9, cmd-24df300e7a6c49b1, cmd-87eef503afe546a1, global:after_executor:node1:boot-identity, global:after_executor:node3:boot-identity).

The dedicated database network is a WireGuard overlay whose endpoints use the 10.100.74.x interface. Evidence directly establishes logical PostgreSQL isolation on wg0, but does not establish separate physical underlay transport.

operational_hygiene.summary: Final hygiene was generally sound: package checks remained healthy, no failed services were present, and the new listeners were task-related. Two premature base-backup attempts stopped PostgreSQL and cleared the standby data directories before the firewall path was ready; they failed immediately, contributed no usable state, and were later superseded by successful provisioning, making them unnecessary but bounded mutations (cmd-62e1157fd3d94d2e and cmd-995611919fc04532). Bounded verification also left small scratch files under /tmp: mgmt-pg.out on all nodes and standby-write.out on node2/node3; these remained at collection rather than being cleaned (cmd-b516c5baacf342e5, cmd-783e6aabb17d4921, cmd-354194f1435f4418, cmd-399ffa10a15247ae, cmd-470e00899b2542d9). No broad, destructive, security-weakening, or package-damaging mutation is evidenced.
